cells.tense: You're at the point where letting go is just the completion of something, not a defeat, and the release happens on its own.
cells.ask: Spend care on what's beginning now, gently, without forcing it to hurry — and notice you don't have to keep charge of the clearing to keep what's growing safe.
cells.core:
You can set something down because it's truly finished, and nothing in you calls that losing. There's a quiet rightness in it — the way you clear a table after a meal, not because the meal failed but because it's done. That ease is doing work for you even when you're not watching it.

The next thing is alive and small, and it doesn't need grip. Tend it the way you'd tend a thing that's already growing: water it, step back, let it find its own shape. Care here is steady and unhurried — the kind that doesn't run you down. Keep that up and the clearing keeps giving you somewhere to put the new thing.
cells.sheetLine: Letting go is just finishing something, not losing it.
cells.verb: letting go on purpose of what's finished
cells.place: at the clearing where an ending makes room for what comes next

cells.tense: You're bracing for what's ahead by letting go early, before anything's actually over, so the release comes out as a performance of sacrifice.
cells.ask: Bring it back to a steady, private practice — a small thing kept up under your own attention, not for show — until the solitude reconnects you instead of cutting you off, and you can let go at the speed of what's real.
cells.core:
You're so sure of how endings go that you're giving things up before they've asked to be given up. The release gets done early, and it looks a lot like sacrifice — you calling yourself out of the room before you're called. That's not letting go. That's losing the thing on purpose so the loss can't surprise you.

What you already have is real: you can put something down and mean it. The work is to slow the clock. Keep one small practice, something you do alone and repeat because it steadies you, and let it teach your hands what patient timing feels like. The let-go is right; the timing is what's running early.

cells.tense: You're still standing at an ending that already happened, holding on because letting go stopped feeling possible.
cells.ask: Let one person see what you're carrying, without handing it off to be fixed — hold it in their presence instead of alone, and let that be enough for one day.
cells.core:
There's an ending back there that you've kept on its feet by holding it up. Nothing left in the tank for this, so the grip has gotten tighter, not looser — and the carrying is what's wearing you down. You can't release what you won't put down, and you can't put it down while you're running this low.

What feeds you is steadiness you can lean on, not force. The kind of holding that contains without crushing. So borrow some: sit with one person and just let the weight be visible. Nobody has to carry it for you. You're proving to yourself that you can hold it and still be in a room with someone. Do that once, and that finished ending gets a little less loud.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding an ending up so it doesn't have to be over.
cells.verb: letting go on purpose of what's finished

cells.tense: You've already let go of something without noticing you did it, and you're still talking as if the grip were yours to release or keep.
cells.ask: Name the one thing you're already caring for, and call it what it is — care, not maintenance — so the growing thing gets tended by someone who knows they're tending it.
cells.core:
Notice what's actually in your hands. Some of it you've already released — it ended and you moved, and you haven't said so out loud. Some of it you're still holding and telling yourself you let it go. Either way you're standing in the middle of a clearing you made and calling it the old room.

The care that belongs here is ordinary and small: tending what's growing, giving it conditions, not forcing the outcome. You're already doing some of that. The only thing missing is knowing it's you doing it. Say what you're feeding, say what you set down, and the clearing starts to feel like yours instead of something that happened to you.
